name: PT Indofood Sukses Makmur Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indofood: a cash-generative food group at a controlled-company price
frontmatter.summary: Indofood operating profit is growing while reported net profit is not, because unrealised FX on a subsidiary dollar bond sits below the EBIT line. The market pays a mid-single-digit multiple for a four-segment food group that leads its categories. We rate it BUY on a target that assumes only a partial re-rating, not convergence to intrinsic value.
thesis: The nine-month update shows sales up and operating profit up, yet net profit flat because of unrealised FX on ICBP dollar bonds; the market is treating a translation loss as an earnings problem [S3].
Indofood earns a high return on invested capital on a mature, brand-led food base, and its maintenance-heavy capex means most operating profit reaches free cash flow [S2].
The four segments do not offset each other cleanly - wheat is a cost with a pass-through lag for Bogasari, and palm is two-sided for a group that sells more refined oil than it grows [S2, F34].
The balance sheet carries net debt of IDR17,650.3bn against EBITDA of IDR28,735.5bn, so the equity is a claim on operating cash flow, not on leverage [S2].
A low payout with a rising dividend record and an announced buyback show capital return is widening without stretching the balance sheet [S4, S6].
The risk is not the business but the multiple - a controlled company with large minorities can stay cheap for years, and our target does not require it to stop being cheap [S2].

catalysts.event: Completion window of the announced share buyback
FY2026 full-year results and the 2027 operating plan
March-quarter CPO and wheat prints that reset input costs
Dividend for book year 2026 declared and paid

blocks.text: We initiate Indofood Sukses Makmur at **BUY** with a target of Rp13,736, 105.2% above the Rp6,875 close on 6 November 2026. The target is a twelve-month value built 60% on P/E at Rp10,485, 25% on EV/EBITDA at Rp11,542 and 15% on the FCFF model at Rp19,516 [S0, S2].

The size of that number needs saying plainly. The DCF is what the whole business is worth if the market one day pays for it; it is not what we expect the shares to do next year. A company controlled by a single shareholder, with IDR4,871.7bn of profit going to minorities, can trade at a third of its cash-flow value for years, and we do not underwrite the closing of that gap. The target therefore leans on the multiples the shares and their peers have actually paid - 8.6x earnings and 6.8x EBITDA - which is already a substantial re-rating from today's 5.6x and 4.4x [S0]. If the multiple does not move at all, the holder still earns the 5.4% dividend yield plus whatever the earnings grow, and that is the floor under the call rather than the thesis.

The variant view is a disagreement about what has gone wrong. The shares sit at 5.6x FY2025 earnings and 0.8x book value and traded between Rp5,900 and Rp7,500 over the past year [S0]. The explanation offered is that net profit stopped growing. That is true at the net line and false at the operating line: in the first nine months of 2026 net sales reached IDR101.49tn and income from operations IDR20.80tn, an operating margin of 20.6% that is the best in years, while profit attributable to the parent held at IDR7.87tn [S3]. The company attributes the gap to higher unrealised foreign-exchange losses on the US dollar bonds issued by its subsidiary ICBP as the rupiah weakened [S3]. A translation loss on debt that funds an Indonesian business is not a deterioration in the franchise, and it reverses when the currency does.

Three things move the value. First the wheat price, because Bogasari mills more grain than any other Indonesian producer and passes the cost through with a lag; the deck carries wheat at 293.5 US dollars a tonne in FY2026E against 195.7 realised in FY2025, easing to 284.1 in the long run [S0, S5]. Second the rupiah, which sets the import cost of that grain and, separately, translates the dollar bonds into a reported gain or loss that the market is reading as earnings [S2, S3]. Third the multiple the market applies to a controlled company, which is the largest single input into our target and the one we can least forecast [S0].

The palm price is not a clean tailwind and we do not model it as one. Agribusiness total sales were IDR21.04tn in FY2025 against own CPO output of 733 thousand tonnes, so the division sells more refined oil than it grows and is a net purchaser of feedstock at the margin [S2]. The model carries a small net CPO cost link and no CPO revenue line: the upside is left out rather than double-counted, and the deck path is shown for reference only.

Indofood is a vertically integrated Indonesian food group organised into four strategic business groups, each with its own management and profit accountability: Consumer Branded Products, Bogasari, Agribusiness and Distribution [S2]. The structure is unusual for a food company because it owns the value chain from wheat milling and palm cultivation through to branded consumer goods and the trucks that deliver them. Consumer Branded Products makes instant noodles, dairy, snack foods, food seasonings, nutrition and special foods and beverages; Bogasari mills wheat into flour and makes pasta, supported by its own shipping and packaging; Agribusiness runs the oil palm estates, mills and the edible oils and fats refineries; Distribution moves Indofood products and third-party goods through the widest network in the country [S2].

On FY2025 external sales of IDR123.49tn, Consumer Branded Products accounted for IDR75.38tn, Bogasari IDR24.50tn, Agribusiness IDR16.19tn and Distribution IDR7.43tn [S2]. Branded consumer goods are therefore the majority of the group, flour and agribusiness are roughly a third between them, and distribution is the smallest external line because most of what it moves is intercompany and eliminated on consolidation. The profit mix is more skewed than the sales mix: Consumer Branded Products earned IDR15.76tn of segment operating profit against IDR2.83tn for Bogasari and IDR4.13tn for Agribusiness [S2].

The competitive position differs by segment. In instant noodles and several branded categories the group is the volume leader, with brands behind decades of distribution investment; management describes maintaining leadership and stable or rising share in its key categories through 2025 [S2]. Bogasari is one of the largest flour millers in the country, with five mills and annual capacity of 4.4 million tonnes [S2], a business whose moat is scale, port logistics and the customer relationships of an industrial supplier rather than brand. Agribusiness manages around 280 thousand hectares of plantations, produced 733 thousand tonnes of CPO in FY2025 and operates refineries that turn it into cooking oil, margarine and shortening under brands including Bimoli [S2]. Distribution is the group internal logistics moat and also a third-party business that earns a fee on other companies products [S2].

The group is controlled. First Pacific Investment Management Limited, an indirect subsidiary of Hong Kong-listed First Pacific Company, held 50.1% of the shares at the end of 2025, with the remainder public [S2]. Anthoni Salim is president director and chief executive and holds interests in First Pacific [S2]. The most important structural fact for a minority holder is that Indofood owns 80.5% of separately listed ICBP, which holds the branded consumer business and most of the group dollar debt, and a majority of the separately listed agribusiness arm [S2]. Consolidated accounts therefore include large minority interests: minorities took IDR4,871.7bn of the IDR15,556.4bn group net profit in FY2025 [S0, S2]. We value the consolidated group and deduct the minorities at their economic share of consolidated equity value rather than at their book balance, because the DCF values the whole business at a multiple of its book equity and a book deduction would leave the parent holding value that belongs to outside shareholders [S0, S2].

Strategy, as management describes it, is to grow volume and share in branded consumer goods, hold the flour conversion margin, expand the agribusiness and edible oils franchise, and defend the distribution network while widening it into modern trade, food service and online ordering [S2]. Capital spending is maintenance-heavy with selective capacity additions, and the group states its intention to keep a healthy balance sheet while balancing market share against profitability [S2].

The domestic operating environment in 2025 was weak for consumer staples and strong for palm. Indonesia grew real GDP by 5.1%, inflation ran at 2.9% driven by food and beverage prices, Bank Indonesia cut its policy rate to 4.8%, and the rupiah averaged 16,475 to the dollar [S2]. Consumer confidence reached a three-year low, and the fast-moving consumer goods industry saw volumes that were essentially flat while value growth decelerated to low single digits [S2, F43]. That is the demand picture our forecast has to respect: a branded food company cannot outgrow the category by much when households are trading down.

The input picture is the opposite. Palm oil prices rose through 2025 and the agri deck carries CPO at 1,135.0 US dollars a tonne for FY2026E against 1,007.0 realised in FY2025, easing to 1,150.0 in the long run [S0]. Wheat is the other side of the trade: the deck has world wheat at 293.5 US dollars a tonne in FY2026E against 195.7 in FY2025, settling at 284.1 later [S0]. For a group that mills more wheat than any other Indonesian producer this is the single most important cost variable, and it is also the one where the company has the least pricing power, because flour is a commodity sold to industrial bakers and noodle makers on contracts.

Indonesia does not grow wheat. The country flour mills buy imported grain, and the industry body agreed with US Wheat Associates to import at least one million tonnes of US wheat a year over the following five years in a deal valued at one and a quarter billion dollars [S5, F47]. The head of the flour mills association who signed that agreement is the same person who sits on the Indofood board [S2, S5]. Read plainly, the arrangement secures supply and hedges a tariff risk, but it does not remove the world price from the cost base, and it does not give Bogasari the ability to pass the whole move through in the same quarter.

The deck macroeconomic path matters because a large part of the group cost of goods is imported or import-linked. The house macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 to the dollar for FY2027E against a 18,103 spot [S0], i.e. continued modest depreciation. That is a headwind to the flour and dairy cost base and a tailwind to the rupiah value of palm exports, and it is also what drives the unrealised FX losses on ICBP dollar bonds that have flattened reported net profit [S3]. We model the currency through the cost link and through the non-operating line rather than as a separate revenue assumption.

Palm deserves its own paragraph because the obvious story is the wrong one. Indofood is not an upstream planter with a leveraged call on the CPO price: Agribusiness grew 733 thousand tonnes of CPO in FY2025 but recorded total sales of IDR21.04tn, which at any plausible realised price implies it sold materially more refined oil than it produced and bought the difference on the open market [S2]. Higher palm prices therefore lift the upstream margin and raise the feedstock cost of the edible oils business, and the group net position is far closer to balanced than an estate owner's. We treat CPO as a modest net cost and leave the revenue upside out of the model entirely.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high in wheat, where a handful of exporting countries and a concentrated milling industry face each other, and low in palm, where the group owns estates. Buyer power is high in flour, where industrial customers negotiate annually, and low in branded noodles, where the brand and the distribution reach do the work. Threat of entry is low in flour and palm, which need capital and land, and moderate in snacks and beverages, where local challengers appear continuously. Substitutes are a slow force in staples and a real one in premium categories as health preferences shift. Rivalry is intense in every segment but is fought on distribution and price points rather than on product novelty [S2].

The moat we are willing to underwrite is distribution density and brand habit in branded consumer goods, and scale plus port logistics in Bogasari. We are not underwriting pricing power in flour, and we are not underwriting palm margins beyond the deck cycle. The method card demand - name the moat mechanism and show evidence it is widening - is only partly met: management claims stable or rising share in key categories [S2], but flat industry volumes [F43] mean the moat is defending a share of a market that is not growing in volume. That is why our long-run revenue growth assumption fades to nominal rather than real-plus-inflation rates.

The first thing a reader should know is that the data pack we start from understates depreciation by a wide margin: the consolidated accounts charge IDR4,017.4bn in FY2024 and IDR4,166.4bn in FY2025 [S0, S2]. We restated both years from the filing, and we took income from operations from the accounts rather than from the pack: IDR23,088.2bn for FY2024 and IDR24,569.1bn for FY2025 [S2]. EBITDA is rebuilt from those lines and now matches the company own financial highlights at IDR28,735.5bn [S2]. The restatement matters for every multiple in this report: the same price is a much cheaper claim on cash flow once the depreciation charge is right.

One artefact survives and the reader should see it. The pack's depreciation for FY2022 and FY2023 is also a fraction of the true charge, and we could not source those two years from an archived filing, so the model EBITDA series breaks upward at FY2024: IDR20,852.7bn and IDR27,105.5bn are not a growth rate, they are an accounting repair. The company own highlights give IDR23,604.4bn for FY2022 and IDR23,572.3bn for FY2023 [S2], i.e. broadly flat, which is the shape of the real history. We flag the break wherever history is described, and we note that the own-history EV/EBITDA benchmark is computed on the pack's understated EBITDA for those years and is therefore if anything too high; the blended multiple we use is the lower for it.

FY2025 was a year of volume-led growth with a margin squeeze from inputs. Revenue rose 6.7% to IDR123.49tn, gross margin narrowed to 33.4% as input costs rose, and operating margin held at 19.9% because selling and distribution costs were contained and other operating income, largely FX gains on operating activities, offset part of the cost increase [S2]. Net profit attributable to the parent was IDR10.68tn, or Rp1,217 per share, of which minorities took IDR4.87tn [S0, S2].

Our forecast starts from the nine-month actual and the company own plan. FY2026E revenue is IDR137.82tn, up 11.6%, which carries the nine-month run-rate of sales at IDR101.49tn against IDR90.98tn a year earlier [S3] through a normal fourth quarter rather than fading in it. Operating profit is IDR28.38tn at a 20.6% margin, in line with the IDR20.80tn nine-month figure [S3]. Beyond FY2026E growth fades toward the long-run rate as the palm cycle normalises and branded food value growth stays in the mid single digits [S2, F43].

The opex line is where a careless model inflates earnings, so we rebuilt it from the notes. Selling and distribution cost was IDR12.59tn and general and administrative cost IDR5.24tn; other operating income was IDR1.99tn, but IDR0.95tn of that was a net FX gain on operating activities against a far smaller figure the year before, and other operating expenses were IDR0.64tn [S2]. We therefore model the SG&A and other-opex line from the two cost lines plus other operating expense and the biological-asset loss, less the recurring part of other operating income but excluding the FX gain, which is not an operating item and which we do not carry forward [S2]. That reproduces the operating margin the nine months actually delivered, and it removes a gain we would otherwise be capitalising forever while separately charging FX losses below the line [S3].

Costs are modelled through two links, not by assumption. Wheat is about a fifth of consolidated cost of goods: Bogasari external sales are IDR24.50tn of a group total of IDR123.49tn, its mills run 4.4 million tonnes of capacity, and its conversion margin is thin, with segment EBIT of IDR2.83tn [S2]. We assume the group passes most of a wheat move through to flour prices with a lag, in line with the company own description that domestic flour prices stayed steady while world wheat fell and the rupiah offset the benefit [S2]. The palm link is deliberately small, and it runs the other way from the obvious story: the group is a net purchaser of refined-oil feedstock at the margin, not a structural long, so a small COGS exposure with half of it passed through is the right order of magnitude and the CPO revenue upside is not counted [S2]. This is the one place where the industry template does not fit the business, and we say so rather than let a mechanical link imply that rising palm prices are a clean tailwind.

Bogasari deserves a separate word because it carries the wheat risk the rest of the group does not. It earned segment EBIT of IDR2.83tn on external sales of IDR24.50tn in FY2025, a conversion margin in the low double digits [S2]. If wheat rises as the deck expects and pass-through lags by a quarter, this segment margin takes the hit while branded goods carry the group. Our bear case does exactly that.

Cash conversion is the heart of the investment case, and it is checkable. Operating cash flow was IDR19.54tn in FY2025 and IDR17.51tn in FY2024, against net profit of IDR15.56tn and IDR13.08tn [S2]. Net profit has been below operating cash flow in both years, so the accruals ratio is negative and earnings are running behind cash, not ahead of it, and the gap has not widened [S2]. Capital expenditure was IDR5.30tn and free cash flow to the firm IDR17.79tn [S0, S2]. Working capital is modest for a food company, IDR16.26tn or about a seventh of sales, because inventories turn and receivables are short [S0]. Trade receivables were IDR10.59tn at the end of FY2025 and, while mostly current, they grew faster than revenue that year, which is a divergence flag we monitor rather than one that has yet cost cash [S2, F1]. The group reports comfortable interest cover and a liabilities-to-equity ratio below one [S2]. We forecast capex of IDR5.93tn against a depreciation charge of IDR4.64tn, which is what a mature manufacturer replacing assets and adding selective capacity spends.

The balance sheet is comfortable, and the two costs of debt are not the same thing. Total funded debt was IDR74.57tn at the end of FY2025 [S2], of which IDR46.15tn of face value is four US dollar bond series maturing between 2031 and 2052 [S2], against cash of IDR57.31tn and EBITDA of IDR28.74tn, so net debt is IDR17.65tn and net debt to EBITDA 0.6x [S0]. We charge interest on the opening balance at the cash coupon the group actually paid, which is well below the marginal cost of refinancing [S2]. The finance expense line of IDR5.97tn is larger than cash interest because it also carries unrealised currency losses and bond-cost amortisation [S2]. We put the rest in other non-operating items at IDR-1.80tn, shrinking as the dollar debt amortises, because that is the line that has flattened reported profit and we would rather show it than wish it away [S3].

Capital allocation is conservative, and the buyback is small. The FY2025 dividend was Rp290 per share, a payout of 24%, with dividends paid of IDR2.46tn [S4, S2]. The record has risen in each of the past several years, and the group announced a buyback alongside ICBP [S4, S6]. At the current market value the programme retires a small slice of the count, and we model it as such rather than as a change of capital-return regime; a payout held at 24% leaves the rest of free cash flow to repay debt and accumulate, which is what the company has done historically and has not said it will stop [S4].

Earnings quality. We ran the house screens. The accruals picture is benign: operating cash flow exceeds net profit and the gap has not widened [S2]. There are no special notation letters, no going-concern language, and the FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified opinion [S2]. The flags we do carry are structural rather than accounting. Related-party sales are 8.4% of consolidated net sales, purchases from related parties 0.5% of cost of goods, and the group both sells to and buys from affiliates in the Salim orbit [S2]; that is a gravity risk to monitor, not a manipulation finding, and we classify it as optics-class. The other flag is the debt structure: a subsidiary issues dollar bonds inside a rupiah-earning group, so reported net profit swings with the currency while operating profit does not [S3]. That too is optics-class, and we model it explicitly rather than adjust it away. The one divergence we did find is receivables growing faster than sales, which we monitor rather than treat as a finding until it shows up in cash [S2, F1].

Against our forecast the nine-month actual is broadly on track. Sales of IDR101.49tn and operating profit of IDR20.80tn are consistent with our full-year numbers, and core profit of IDR9.37tn - the company own measure, which strips the currency noise - grew at a rate close to our earnings forecast [S3]. The miss, if there is one, will be at the net line and will come from the currency, not from the business.

We use FCFF as the fundamental method because Indofood is a cash-generative, capital-intensive food manufacturer with a stable capital structure and a predictable reinvestment need. A discounted cash flow captures the two things a multiple cannot: the durability of the operating margin across a palm and wheat cycle, and the fact that the group minorities take a fixed share of consolidated profit. We do not weight it heavily in the twelve-month target, and the reason is arithmetic rather than aesthetic: at a 11.2% cost of capital with 3.5% terminal growth the model terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA above the 6.8x the cross-check uses, which is the multiple expansion the method card warns about [S0]. A market that has paid 4.4x for this cash flow is not going to pay the DCF exit multiple within a year, so we hold the DCF as the value of the business and build the target out of the multiples the shares actually trade at [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house frame and disclosed in full. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the country risk premium 2.5% and the industry unlevered beta 0.70, relevered to a 1.29 debt-to-equity ratio to give a levered beta of 1.40 [S0]. With a governance premium of 1.0% - justified by the controlled ownership, the related-party flows and the minority structure described in section six - the cost of equity is 16.2% [S2]. The cost of debt is 9.4% pre-tax, the forward risk-free-plus-spread rate the house frame applies to an Indonesian issuer and deliberately higher than the coupon the model charges on the existing stack, which was issued at low fixed rates and is not what refinancing costs today [S2, F59]. At market weights of 43.7% equity and 56.3% debt the weighted average cost of capital is 11.2%, inside the house band for rupiah names [S0].

The enterprise value from the model is IDR265,993.7bn, of which 50.5% sits in the terminal value [S0]. That is a normal share for a ten-year explicit forecast, but the reader should know what it implies: the terminal value capitalises the final year at the discount rate less the terminal growth rate, and the multiple that falls out is above both the twelve-month cross-check and today price. We accept it as a statement of value, not as a forecast of the price, and the sensitivity table shows how much of the DCF depends on that assumption.

The growth arithmetic passes the card first test once it is stated honestly. Reinvestment - capex less depreciation plus the change in working capital - is a modest share of after-tax operating profit, and at the returns the group earns on invested capital that reinvestment funds real volume growth of a couple of points a year. The rest of our nominal growth is price, which needs no capital, and the fade to the long-run rate reflects the flat industry volumes the company itself reports [S2, F43]. We do not claim a widening moat; we claim a durable one defending a mature market, which is why growth fades and margins hold rather than expand.

The cross-checks do not tell the same story, and we do not smooth it. P/E at Rp10,485 uses 8.6x and EV/EBITDA at Rp11,542 uses 6.8x, against today 5.6x and 4.4x [S0]. Both are averages of the peer median and the group own five-year history, so both already assume a re-rating to roughly half the gap, and they still land below the DCF. We keep the weights because the house requires a market-anchored cross-check, and we report the gap rather than hide it; the honest reading is that every method in this report assumes the market pays more for this cash flow than it does today, and the disagreement is only about how much.

The minority deduction is where a consolidated DCF usually overstates the parent claim, so we mark it at value rather than at book. Minorities took IDR4,871.7bn of IDR15,556.4bn group net profit, and the DCF values the consolidated business at a multiple of its book equity, so deducting the book minority balance alone would leave the parent holding a value that belongs to ICBP and the agribusiness arm outside shareholders [S0, S2]. We therefore carry an additional deduction in the bridge, sized at the minorities economic share of consolidated equity value, and we state the basis here because it is a judgement rather than a disclosure.

The reverse calculation is the cleanest statement of the gap, provided it is read correctly. The engine solves for a single shift applied to revenue growth in every forecast year, not a one-year dip: at today price the required shift gives growth of -2.7% a year for a decade [S0]. That is what a permanent contraction looks like, and nothing in the nine-month results supports it - sales grew, operating profit grew faster, and the only line that did not grow was the one carrying an unrealised currency loss [S3]. Either the market knows something about the durability of the palm and flour margins that we do not, or it is applying a discount for control and minority structure that will not narrow until the ownership does.

Two honest caveats. The first is that 50.5% of our DCF is terminal, so a reader who thinks the long-run margin should be below the FY2025 actual can discount that leg heavily; the sensitivity table shows how much. The second is that the discount rate is the lever we are least sure of: each point on the cost of equity removes a meaningful slice of the DCF, and a market that demands a higher return from a family-controlled Indonesian food company is not irrational, merely expensive for the holder.
We rank the downside risks by likelihood and impact, and we name the ones that would change the rating rather than the ones that make a long list.

Regulatory and policy risk is medium likelihood and medium impact. Flour is a staple with price sensitivity, and any move to cap flour or cooking-oil prices would hit the two segments that carry the group commodity exposure [S2]. The wheat import arrangement with the US is a supply hedge but ties the group to a political bargain that can be renegotiated [S5].

Commodity risk is high likelihood and medium impact, because it is already in the deck. Wheat is projected to rise sharply in FY2026E before easing, and a pass-through lag would compress the Bogasari margin for a quarter or two [S0, S2]. Palm is a smaller and two-sided exposure for the reason section two sets out: a higher CPO price helps the upstream margin and hurts the edible oils margin, and the net position is close to balanced [S2].

Currency risk is high likelihood and high impact on reported earnings, and it is the risk we can size. The parent carries IDR46.15tn of face value in dollar bonds and the subsidiary carries more, so a sharp move in the rupiah is a translation swing of the same order as a year of the other non-operating charge we model [S2, F59]. The rupiah has already moved, the house deck expects more of it, and the FY2025 comparison shows the average rate moving with the year-end rate [S2, S3, S0]. This is the risk that has already done the damage to the share price and the one we think is most misread, but it is a real risk to next year net profit and dividend coverage, not a cosmetic one.

Operational risk is low likelihood and medium impact: a food recall, a fire at a mill or a distribution disruption would hit a segment volumes for a season. The group scale and multiple plants mitigate it, and there is no evidence of a current problem [S2].

Governance and structure risk is medium likelihood and high impact on the multiple. The controlling shareholder holds 50.1%, related-party sales are 8.4% of revenue, and the group is a collection of listed and unlisted entities with large minorities [S2]. A transaction that moves value between those entities would hurt minorities, and the discount the market applies is partly a price for that risk. We do not forecast a related-party event; we apply a governance premium in the cost of equity and hold most of the target on multiples rather than on the DCF precisely because that discount can persist.
Liquidity risk is low. The shares trade a healthy daily value, and the free float is 48.5% [S0]. A holder can build and exit a position, which is why the target carries no liquidity haircut.

The scenarios are mirrored and each shocks the same four drivers in opposite directions: revenue growth, gross margin, other non-operating items and the cost of equity. In the bear the discount does not narrow - volumes stall, the margin compresses, the rupiah keeps translating the dollar bonds into losses and the market demands a higher return from a controlled company; in the bull the same four move the other way, reflecting a consumer recovery, a currency that stops falling and a market willing to pay a normal food multiple [S2]. The probabilities give the base case most of the weight and the bear slightly more than the bull, because the currency has been moving against the group rather than for it [S0, S3].

Two limits of the table should be stated rather than discovered. First, the multiple methods hold the same benchmark multiple in every scenario, so the table prices an operating bear but not a de-rating: the case where the shares simply keep today 4.4x is worse than our bear, and it is the case the market has been in for five years [S0]. Second, because the shares are already at a decade-low multiple, even the bear values them above today price; the call therefore does not depend on the discount closing, and the honest test of it is the earnings themselves.

Signposts that would change our view: a fall in the operating margin below the level the group held through the weak consumer year, which would say the brands are losing pricing; a related-party transaction that transfers a material asset at anything other than arm length; a dividend cut or a buyback funded with debt; and a sustained rupiah appreciation that removes the currency drag and shows what the underlying earnings growth actually is [S2, S3]. The last is the one we would most like to see, because it would force the market to re-price the net line.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. First Pacific Investment Management Limited held 50.1% at the end of 2025, unchanged through the year, and the public held the rest, with foreign institutions the largest public block [S2]. Anthoni Salim is president director and chief executive and holds interests in First Pacific, so control and management sit in the same hands [S2]. The free float of 48.5% is above the exchange minimum, and there is no special-monitoring notation or going-concern flag on the name [S0, S2].

Related-party dealings are the governance issue to watch, not a finding of abuse. Sales to related parties were 8.4% of consolidated net sales in FY2025 and purchases from related parties 0.5% of cost of goods, and the company states that these were on arm length terms [S2]. The pattern is normal for a family-controlled Indonesian group with affiliated distribution and logistics businesses; the risk is that the terms drift. We monitor the disclosure each year rather than assume either the best or the worst.

The board and audit arrangements are conventional. The FY2025 consolidated statements were audited by Purwantono, Sungkoro and Surja with an unmodified opinion, and the same firm was reappointed for the following year [S2]. There is an audit committee and a commissioner structure with independent members, and the annual report discloses its composition and attendance [S2]. We found no pledged-share disclosure for the controlling stake in the annual report, and no serial rights issuance: the share count has been stable at 8,780 million shares [S2, S4].

The dividend record is the clearest evidence of minority-friendly capital allocation. The group paid Rp290 per share for book year 2025 after Rp280 a year earlier, a payout of 24% that has been consistent for several years [S4]. The announced buyback alongside ICBP, sized at a meaningful but not transformative amount, is a second channel [S6].

ESG exposure is dominated by palm. The group publishes a standalone sustainability report and states that most nucleus CPO production is Indonesian Sustainable Palm Oil certified, with the balance of the estate and mill network on a path to certification [S2, S7]. That matters commercially because export customers and financiers increasingly require it, and it matters reputationally because palm deforestation is the sector principal controversy. The other exposures - water and effluent at the mills, labour standards on the estates, packaging - are disclosed and managed, and the group reports on them at manufacturing-unit level [S7]. On the consumer side, nutrition and sugar content is a slow-moving regulatory and reputational risk for the beverage and dairy lines [S2].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the completion window of the announced buyback, the FY2026 results and 2027 plan in the March reporting season, the dividend for book year 2026 in the middle of next year, and the quarterly commodity prints that reset the two cost links [S4, S5, S6]. We would add the quarterly ICBP disclosures, because that is where the dollar debt and the currency line are reported and where the market confusion about the net line originates [S3].

Between updates we monitor five things. First, the consolidated operating margin against the level the group held in the weak consumer year - it is the single best test of whether the brands are defending price [S2]. Second, Bogasari segment margin against the wheat price, which tells us whether pass-through is holding [S2, S0]. Third, the difference between Agribusiness segment profit and the CPO price, which tells us how much of the group growth is franchise and how much is feedstock timing [S2, S0]. Fourth, related-party sales as a share of revenue, which is the governance tripwire [S2]. Fifth, the gap between core profit and reported net profit, which is the currency line and the thing the market is currently mispricing [S3].

Indofood is one of the oldest and most recognisable consumer franchises in Indonesia, and its noodles are part of the everyday diet in a way that is hard to convey with financial statements. The group history runs through several name changes and a period of expansion into packaging, agribusiness and distribution that made it a vertically integrated food company rather than a single-category brand owner. Its controlling shareholder is a Hong Kong-listed conglomerate with interests across telecoms, infrastructure and consumer goods in Southeast Asia. Like many Indonesian family-controlled groups, it has a history of related-party arrangements that analysts have debated for years, and like many of them it trades at a discount to what a pure-play food company would command.

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for INDF.JK

valuation.label: P/E
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

valuation.label: EV/EBITDA
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: The discount does not narrow. Consumer staples volumes stall as real incomes stay weak, wheat and CPO stay elevated so the gross margin compresses, the rupiah keeps translating ICBP's dollar bonds into unrealised losses and the market demands a higher return from a controlled company, so the shares stay near the current multiple for a second year.

bull.narrative: The discount narrows. A rupiah recovery cuts the FX drag on ICBP's dollar bonds, wheat falls back with the world crop, mid-single-digit FMCG volume growth plus firm CPO lift both CBP and Agribusiness, and the market pays a normal food multiple for the earnings, taking the EBIT margin back above 21%.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 consolidated sales rose 11.6% yoy to Rp101.49trn [F27, F45, S3], with operating profit up 15% at a 20.5% margin [F28, S3]; FY2025 growth was 6.6% on all four segments [S2]. FY2026E +11.6% holds the nine-month run-rate through a normal fourth quarter; FY2027E +6.0% assumes FMCG value growth of mid-single digits (2025 industry volume was flat, value growth low-single-digit [S2 p.23]) plus mid-single-digit agribusiness on the deck's firm CPO path; then fades to +4.5% long run in line with Indonesian nominal consumption growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 LK gross margin 33.4% (Rp41.19trn on Rp123.49trn) [F1, S2 p.152], down from 34.7% on higher input costs. The input margin is stated before the wheat and CPO links. FY2026E is set so the modelled EBIT margin reproduces the nine-month actual: 9M2026 sales Rp101.49trn and operating profit Rp20.80trn is a 20.5% margin [F27, F28, S3], and with the opex line at 14.24% of sales that implies a gross margin in the mid-thirties. The margin then holds as wheat normalises to the deck's long-run price [S0, S5].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: CPO enters the model as a cost only. Agribusiness total sales were Rp21.04trn in FY2025 [F34, S2 p.63] against own CPO output of 733kt [F24, S2 p.63], so the division sells more CPO-equivalent than it grows and is a net purchaser of refined-oil feedstock at the margin; the group's exposure is therefore two-sided, not the structural long-palm position an upstream planter has. The template has no CPO revenue line, so this 5% of COGS with 50% pass-through is the only modelled channel and the CPO upside is deliberately not counted.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Cooking-oil and margarine prices track CPO with a short lag; the group raised edible-oil prices through 2025 as CPO rose and still lifted volumes [S2 p.63-64]. 50% pass-through leaves half of the small net purchased exposure in the margin.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Wheat is Bogasari's dominant raw material. Bogasari external sales were Rp24.50trn of Rp123.49trn consolidated [F11, S2 p.291], its five mills run 4.4Mt of annual capacity [F23], and flour milling is a low-margin conversion business (segment EBIT Rp2.83trn [F15]); wheat is therefore about 18% of consolidated COGS.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: The AR states domestic flour prices held steady in 2025 as lower world wheat prices were offset by a weaker rupiah's import cost [S2 p.23], i.e. Bogasari passes input moves through with a lag. 85% pass-through keeps the conversion margin broadly stable, leaving 15% of the wheat move in gross profit.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from the LK note 28 components: selling & distribution Rp12,591.6bn (10.20% of sales) plus general & administrative Rp5,244.8bn (4.25%) plus other operating expenses Rp644.7bn (0.52%) plus the biological-asset loss Rp135.5bn (0.11%), less recurring other operating income of Rp1,041.1bn (0.84%) - total other operating income Rp1,993.3bn less the Rp952.2bn net FX gain on operating activities [F53, F54, F55, F56, F57, S2 p.152, p.270]. That is 14.24% of sales. The FX gain is excluded because it was Rp78bn in FY2024 and is not a recurring operating item; the operating FX gain is not carried into the forecast, and the bond-translation loss is modelled separately in other non-operating items. Held flat.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from LK note 36: D&A Rp4,166.4bn on revenue Rp123,493.2bn = 3.37% [F4, F1, S2]. The data pack's Rp715bn was a fraction of the real charge; the engine now rebuilds EBITDA from the filing (EBITDA Rp28.7trn, matching the AR's financial highlights).

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: LK cash-flow additions to fixed assets, plantations and advances were Rp5,295.2bn in FY2025 and Rp5,417.1bn in FY2024 [F6, F7, S2], 4.3% of sales - mostly maintenance plus noodle, dairy and packaging capacity. Held at 4.3%, just above the 3.4% D&A charge, which is consistent with a mature food manufacturer growing volumes mid-single digit.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was 13.2% of sales and FY2024 13.9% [S0]; 13.5% holds the two-year average. Inventory (grain and CPO stocks) and receivables are the swing items.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 LK: tax Rp4,481.3bn on pre-tax profit Rp20,037.7bn = 22.4%, close to the 22% statutory rate plus minor permanent differences [S2 p.152]. 23% is used.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Cash finance costs paid were Rp4,116.0bn in FY2025 against Rp71,025.4bn opening debt = 5.8% [S2 p.155]; total funded debt Rp74.57trn at end-2025 [F31]. This is the contractual cash coupon on the existing stack (four US dollar series at 3.4-4.8% plus rupiah bank debt [F59, S2 p.252]), not the marginal cost: the WACC's kd of 9.45% is the forward risk-free-plus-spread rate the house frame applies when the group refinances. The LK's Rp5,973.9bn finance expense line also carries unrealised FX and amortisation, which is not a cost of debt [F58]. 5.7% used for the interest line.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income Rp1,662.9bn on Rp48,225.0bn opening cash = 3.4% [S2 p.152]. 3.5% used.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new net debt assumed: funded debt rose only Rp3.8trn in FY2025 and net debt is roughly flat against a large cash balance (cash Rp61.6trn at 30 Sep 2026) [S0].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Historic other non-operating is a plug (pbt - ebit + interest expense - interest income) of about Rp2.1trn a year: the part of finance expense that is not cash interest - unrealised FX on the US dollar bonds and bond-cost amortisation [F58, S2 p.152]. It stays in the forecast because 9M2026 net profit was held flat by a larger unrealised FX loss as the rupiah weakened [F29, S3], and the house macro deck still has usd_idr at 18,350 for FY2027E. Modelled at Rp1.8trn and shrinking as the dollar debt amortises.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minorities took Rp4,871.7bn of Rp15,556.4bn net profit = 31.3%, reflecting the 19.5% of ICBP and 25.7% of Indofood Agri not owned [F21, S2 p.6, p.132]. Held at 31.3%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS Rp290 on EPS Rp1,217 = 24% payout [F8, F32, S4]; the record runs 24-29% since 2023. 25% assumed, with the rest funding capex and the announced buyback. The company has not guided to a higher payout, so the accumulating cash is left in the model and returned to the holder only through the buyback below (see the capital-return note in section three).

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The announced Rp750bn buyback [S6] is 1.2% of the market capitalisation at the current price, so FY2026E carries a 1.2% reduction in the count; afterwards flat, because the programme size is fixed and treasury shares are not cancelled [S4, S6]. Shares issued and fully paid are 8,780,426,500 [F9].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.5% in rupiah: above the house macro deck's long-run Indonesian inflation, below Indonesian long-run nominal GDP (real growth plus inflation in the house macro deck), so the terminal value implies a lower exit multiple than 4% while still respecting the no-fade-above-GDP rule for a mature food manufacturer whose volume growth tracks population and income [S0].

challenges.challenge: The 233.4% expected return is the size of the discount, not an expected return. The report and the extreme_call justification both say the gap is a control/minority/illiquidity discount and that "our base case does not assume it closes", yet the target is a full fundamental value rolled forward at COE with liquidity_discount 0.0% and only a 1.0pp COE governance premium (worth about 8% of DCF value) against a 70% price-to-fundamental-value gap. ADTV is Rp43.7bn a day, so illiquidity is not an explanation. If the discount persists the holder earns the 5.0% yield plus growth, not 233%, and the BUY rating is derived from a number that is not a 12-month return.
challenges.answer: Target no longer rolled full fundamental value: weights P/E 60%, EV/EBITDA 25%, DCF 15% give Rp13,736 and 105.2% TR; report now states the DCF is business value, not next-year return, and that the discount is not assumed to close [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is misstated. The engine shocks a.revenue_growth across the whole forecast dict (cov_engine Model._apply_overrides), so the stated FY2027 revenue growth of -7.1% is in fact -7.1% every year from FY2026E to FY2035E, a permanent contraction, not one year. The sensitivity table shows -4pp every year costs 31% of target, so a single year at -7% would move it about 1-2%, not the 72% needed to reach the price. The report calls this its cleanest statement of the opportunity and repeats it in the QC justification.
challenges.answer: Reverse DCF restated as a permanent shift applied to every forecast year (implied -2.7% growth a year for a decade), reconciled to the sensitivity grid, and reworded in section 4 and the extreme_call justification [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bridge deducts minorities at book (Rp49,264.5bn, market.minority_bs) although those minorities take 31.3% of net profit and the DCF values the consolidated business at 2.7x book. A consistent deduction is 31.3% of the DCF equity value, about Rp67.2trn, which cuts the DCF from Rp24,445 to about Rp22,400 and the scenario-weighted target by roughly Rp1,400 (-6%) to about Rp21,150. The same book figure is used in the P/E and EV/EBITDA bridges, and the basis is never stated.
challenges.answer: Minorities now deducted at their economic share of consolidated equity value through a Rp33.3trn bridge item on top of the book figure; basis stated in sections 1 and 4 and the deduction disclosed in table:valuation [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: The terminal value of Rp384,072bn is 8.38x FY2035 EBITDA and 9.90x FY2035 EBIT, above both the 6.82x the report itself uses as a fair multiple (half peer median, half own five-year average) and the 4.43x entry multiple in its own table. The only justification is that the market multiple is not a fair-value benchmark, which assumes the conclusion. At a 6.82x exit the DCF is about Rp21,370 and the target about Rp20,400 - still a BUY, so the rating survives but the DCF leg is overstated by about 16%.
challenges.answer: DCF weight cut to 15% so the exit multiple is a disclosed value statement not the target driver; section 4 states the implied exit multiple sits above the 6.82x cross-check and that the sensitivity table carries the dependency [S0].

challenges.challenge: The claim that Indofood is structurally long palm is unsourced and contradicted by the data cited. Agribusiness total sales were Rp21.04trn (S2 p.31/63) against 733kt of own CPO (F24); at the FY2025 realised USD1,007/t and Rp16,475 that output is worth about Rp12.2trn, so the division sells roughly 1.0-1.3mt of CPO-equivalent against 733kt produced, a net purchased position. The model only CPO channel is a 5% COGS cost link, so the price called the first value driver in the summary has no revenue line at all and a higher CPO price is modelled as a small cost, not a tailwind.
challenges.answer: Long-palm claim deleted from summary, section 2 and section 3; Agribusiness sales of Rp21.04trn against 733kt own CPO is now shown as a net purchased refined-oil position with only a small cost link and no CPO revenue line [S2, F24, F34].

challenges.challenge: The base case cuts FY2026 below the nine-month actual without a source. 9M2026 EBIT was Rp20.80trn at a 20.5% margin (S3), but FY2026E is Rp26.90trn at 19.8%, implying Q4 EBIT of Rp6.10trn versus Rp6.47trn in Q4 2025 (-5.7%) on revenue +5.7% yoy, a 17.8% Q4 margin against 19.9% a year earlier. FY2026E revenue growth of 10.0% also sits below the 9M +11.6%. The method card prohibits default haircuts. Holding the Q4 margin at the 9M level adds about Rp0.9trn of EBIT, roughly 3% of target.
challenges.answer: FY2026E growth raised to 11.6% and gross margin set so EBIT is 20.6% of sales, holding the 9M2026 20.5% margin through a normal fourth quarter rather than implying a contraction [S3, F27, F28].

challenges.challenge: Two costs of debt in one report, unreconciled and undisclosed. The WACC uses kd_pre_tax 9.45% (rf 7.45% plus a default spread) and a 56.3% debt weight, while the model cost_of_debt is 5.7% and the LK finance expense of Rp5,973.9bn on Rp74,570bn of funded debt is 8.0%. At an 8.0% pre-tax kd the WACC falls about 0.6pp to 10.6%, which the sensitivity grid says adds roughly 12% to the DCF. Section 4 lists rf, ERP, CRP and beta but never the cost of debt or the weights.
challenges.answer: Full WACC build now disclosed in section 4 with kd_pre_tax 9.4%, we 43.7% and wd 56.3%; section 3 reconciles the 5.7% cash coupon on the existing stack to the higher marginal refinancing rate used in WACC [S2, F59].

challenges.challenge: The D&A restatement stops at FY2024. FY2022A (825.7) and FY2023A (714.4) still carry the pack figure while FY2024/25 use the LK 4,017/4,166, so the model EBITDA history reads 19,754 / 20,853 / 27,106 / 28,735, a 30% FY2024 jump that is an accounting artifact, not growth. Those two years also feed the own five-year EV/EBITDA mean of 5.91x, half of the 6.82x cross-check multiple, inflating that leg by roughly 7%.
challenges.answer: FY2022-23 D&A not extractable from the archived FY2023 report, which carries no financial statements; company EBITDA of F48 and F49 is disclosed and section 3 states the series break and that the own-history multiple is computed on understated EBITDA and is therefore too high [S2, F48, F49].

challenges.challenge: The scenario framework cannot change the rating, so it does not test the thesis. Bear is Rp16,735 (+143% from the price) and bull Rp29,302; doubling the bear probability to 50% still gives Rp21,228 (+209%). No scenario shocks the discount rate or terminal growth, although Section 4 calls the discount rate the lever we are least sure of, and no scenario models the one outcome the report itself says explains the price: the control/minority discount persisting.
challenges.answer: Scenarios now shock val.coe by 1.5pp and other_nonop by 500 in both directions, so the discount rate and the FX line move; section 5 states the multiple methods hold the multiple constant, so the bear understates a de-rating and the call does not depend on the discount closing [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: Indofood owns 80.5% of separately listed ICBP and a majority of separately listed Indofood Agri (F21, S2), yet the report rejects a sum-of-the-parts in one sentence (already inside the consolidation) and never tests whether the consolidated DCF understates or overstates the listed stakes. A SOTP at the subsidiary market values would show directly how much of the 233% gap is a parent-level holdco discount, the report own explanation for the price, and would be the cleanest way to test it.
challenges.answer: The corporate template in cov_engine does not permit an sotp method, so an SOTP cannot be run on this name; the consolidated DCF less minorities at their economic share gives the same parent claim, and the basis is now stated in sections 1 and 4 [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: Capital return is assumed away in the direction that matters least for the target. The model holds payout at 25% and share_change at 0.0 while net debt falls from Rp17.65trn to net cash of Rp17.8trn by FY2028; the Rp750bn buyback (S6) buys about 1.2% of the count at the current price and is not reflected, and no special dividend or higher payout is modelled. The cash builds at a 3.5% yield while the equity costs 16.2%.
challenges.answer: Buyback now modelled as a 1.2% share reduction in FY2026E with no new net debt, and section 3 states the payout policy the company has actually held rather than an assumed special return [S4, S6].

challenges.challenge: FX is named as the risk that has already done the damage but appears in no scenario. ICBP USD debt is Rp77.8trn at 30 Sep 2026; a 10% rupiah move is about Rp7.8trn pre-tax, four times the -Rp1.8trn other_nonop line being modelled, and FY2025 itself moved from 16,475 to 18,103 (+9.9%). The deck FY2027E 18,350 is only +1.4% from spot, so the base case assumes the FX drag shrinks and no case assumes it repeats.
challenges.answer: FX now enters the bear and bull through other_nonop plus or minus 500 and the cost of equity; section 5 sizes the exposure from the Rp46.2trn parent dollar bonds and the 9M2026 flat net profit despite higher operating profit [S2, F59, S3].

challenges.challenge: The opex plug permanently embeds other operating income. The basis says S&D 10.2% + G&A 4.2% less other operating income 1.6% = 13.46%, but that arithmetic gives 12.8%; the LK (S2 p.152) shows S&D Rp12,591.6bn (10.20%) and G&A Rp5,244.8bn (4.25%), implying other operating income of about Rp1,213bn (0.98%), not 1.6%. The 13.46% plug then carries about Rp1.2trn a year of largely FX gains as a fixed share of sales forever, while FX losses are separately modelled at -Rp1.8trn. If the gains mean-revert, EBIT falls about 5% and the DCF about 7-8%.
challenges.answer: Opex rebuilt from note 28 components: S&D 10.20% plus G&A 4.25% plus other opex 0.52% plus bio loss 0.11% less recurring other income 0.84% equals 14.24%, excluding the Rp952.2bn FX gain; section 3 sets out the arithmetic and the exclusion [S2, F53 to F57].

challenges.challenge: The cross-check paragraph misdescribes its own inputs: P/E at Rp10,485 and EV/EBITDA at Rp15,338 are said to capitalise the depressed multiple. The multiples used are 8.62x and 6.82x, while the current ones are 5.65x FY2025A and 4.43x (model multiple table), so both cross-checks already assume a 53-54% re-rating to peer/history levels and still land 57% and 37% below the DCF. Presenting them as the current multiple hides that every method assumes some re-rating.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the multiples used (8.6x and 6.8x) against current 5.6x and 4.4x and says explicitly that all three methods assume some re-rating, rather than calling them the depressed multiple [S0].

challenges.challenge: The house earnings-quality screen is asserted, not shown. Section 3 says the accruals picture is benign and receivables did not outrun revenue but gives no three-year accruals ratio, no cash-conversion trend and no manipulation-class versus optics-class classification, which the method card requires as the output contract. The conclusion may well be right (OCF exceeds net profit), but a reader cannot verify it from the report.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now carries operating cash flow against net profit for FY2024 and FY2025, the receivables divergence flag and an explicit optics-class versus manipulation-class classification per the method card [S2, F51, F52].

missing_bull_case.note: No sum-of-the-parts for the 80.5% listed ICBP stake and the listed Indofood Agri majority (C10), and no case for the Rp17.8trn of net cash the model builds by FY2028 being returned (C11); the report dismisses the SOTP in one sentence without testing it.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear only shocks revenue growth -3pp and gross margin -1.5pp and still returns +143%, so no scenario produces anything but BUY; there is no discount-persists branch, no WACC/terminal-g shock, and no FX stress despite USD debt of Rp77.8trn (C9, C12).

assumption_realism.note: The "structurally long palm" basis for the 5% CPO link is unsourced and contradicted by the segment data (C5); FY2026E embeds an unsourced Q4 margin cut to 17.8% (C6); and the opex plug carries about Rp1.2trn a year of FX gains as a permanent percentage of sales (C13).

evidence_and_citations.note: Six spot-checks passed (F1/F2/F4 on S2 p.152, S3 9M EBIT 20.80, F34 21.04trn, F26/F24 280k ha and 733kt, Welirang board seat S2 p.10). Fails on the D&A restatement left half-done for FY2022-23 (C8) and on the earnings-quality screen not being quantified (C15). Free float is 48.5% in the report vs 49.91% in S2 p.10.

valuation_method_fit.note: The named bridge deducts minorities at book (Rp49.3trn) while the DCF marks the group at 2.7x book, worth about -6% of target (C3); the terminal value implies 8.4x EBITDA against the report own 6.82x fair multiple (C4); the reverse DCF misstates its own shock (C2); and the WACC uses a 9.45% cost of debt while the model uses 5.7% (C7). No reinvestment/ROIIC or terminal ROIC is stated, as the compounder card requires.

bias_and_tone.note: The most important one: the report says "our base case does not assume the discount closes" and then prints a 233.4% expected return that is exactly the discount closing with a 0.0% liquidity discount (C1). The cross-check paragraph also calls 8.62x and 6.82x "the depressed multiple" when the current ones are 5.65x and 4.43x (C14).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: CPO 1,135 and wheat 293.5 match the agri deck and are wired through the COGS link, but CPO enters only as a cost, never as the revenue tailwind the summary names as the first driver; and the USD/IDR path (18,350 FY2027E) is cited but is not a model input, so the rupiah never reaches the dollar-denominated wheat cost (C5).

conservatism_audit.note: Below the 9M actual without a source: FY2026E revenue growth 10.0% vs 9M +11.6%, EBIT margin 19.8% vs 20.5%, implied Q4 EBIT -5.7% yoy at a 17.8% margin vs 19.9% (C6). The WACC 9.45% cost of debt is above both the 5.7% used in the model and the 8.0% the LK shows, which understates the DCF (C7). Scenarios are mirrored in shocks, which is credit.

calibration.note: The engine calibration passes: FY2025A EBITDA margin 23.27% model vs 23.27% actual, gap -0.09pp, and EBITDA of Rp28,735.5bn rebuilt from F2+F4 matches the FY2025 result. The only BLOCK flag is extreme_call, justified with three sourced facts, though the third (reverse DCF) is misstated (C2).

signoff.notes: APPROVED at sign-off (initiation, round 1). FATAL C1 (the 233% expected return was the size of the discount) is properly answered: the target is now 60% P/E / 25% EV/EBITDA / 15% DCF at Rp13,736 and the DCF is stated as business value, not next-year return. All FATAL/MATERIAL challenges are answered on substance; QC, facts and lint PASS. Three QC FIX items remain: Q1 - section 3's claim that FY2022-23 D&A is unsourceable is wrong: S8 p.6 gives EBITDA (23,572.3 / 23,604.4) and EBIT (19,663.6 / 19,693.1), so D&A is derivable (3,908.7 / 3,911.3); state that, or state the two-year restatement-window constraint, and correct the direction of the 'blended multiple is lower for it' sentence - the correction lowers the own-history multiple and the target by roughly 1.7%; Q2 - the disclosed COE build must include the sovereign default-spread term so the 7.4% + 1.07 x (4.2% + 2.5%) + 1.0% build reconciles to the 16.2% used; Q3 - the summary and section 3 still print 20.6% for the 9M2026 operating margin; S3 says 20.5% (20.80/101.49 = 20.49%), and 20.6% belongs only to the FY2026E forecast. Cross-name consistency (desk): INDF owns 80.5% of ICBP, which we also cover BUY. At our ICBP target of Rp14,229 the stake alone is worth about Rp15,200 per INDF share (0.805 x 14,229 x 11,661.9m / 8,780.4m), above INDF's Rp13,736 target, so the pair implies a holdco discount that deepens from about a 2% premium to the stake at market to about 10% at target. That is directionally consistent with the governance discount the report leans on, but it must be stated in section 4 so a reader holding both reports sees why a 13.9x ICBP becomes an 8.6x parent; it does not block the BUY. Batch note as ICBP: the buy-side tilt across the industry comes from the market de-rating, not from the shared deck or discount rate.

bias.note: Operating drivers are anchored to the last actual and the company's plan: FY2026E revenue +11.6% and EBIT margin 20.6% reproduce 9M2026 sales Rp101.49trn / operating profit Rp20.80trn (S3); calibration gap 0.69pp and no drift flags; D&A, capex, opex and tax restated from the LK (S2). The 60% P/E weight at 8.62x vs 5.65x today and 25% EV/EBITDA at 6.82x vs 4.43x embed a ~53% partial re-rating sourced from peer median 9.83x and own five-year 7.41x (S0), disclosed in section 4. Scenarios are mirrored (four shocks each) with base 45%. Direction neutral on the operating case; the multiple re-rating is disclosed but the distribution is one-sided (see Q6).

recomputed.item: FY2025A net debt (funded debt 74,570 less cash 47,471 + STI 9,837)

findings.finding: Section 3 says the FY2022-23 D&A could not be sourced from an archived filing, but S8 (FY2023 annual report, archived) p.6 financial highlights disclose EBITDA (FY2023 23,572.3; FY2022 23,604.4) and EBIT (19,663.6; 19,693.1), so D&A is derivable (3,908.7; 3,911.3). The model's FY2022A/FY2023A EBITDA of 19,754.4/20,852.7 understate the company's own figures by 16.3%/11.5% and feed the pack own-history EV/EBITDA mean (5.91x) that carries 25% of the target; section 3's 'the blended multiple we use is the lower for it' has the direction wrong (correcting the data lowers the multiple, and with it the target by roughly 1.7%).

Section 4's disclosed COE build is 7.4% + 1.40 x (4.2% + 2.5%) + 1.0% = 17.78%, not the 16.2% used. The engine computes COE = rf - default_spread + beta x (ERP + CRP) + premium, i.e. it subtracts a 1.62% default spread from the 7.45% rf. The 16.2% is the correct engine output and reconciles to the 11.2% WACC, so the defect is disclosure, not the target arithmetic (judge FIX, accepted).

The summary and section 3 describe the nine-month 2026 operating margin as 20.6%, but S3 reports 20.5% and 20.80/101.49 = 20.49%; 20.6% is the FY2026E model margin pulled into a sentence about the actual.

Section 3 says funded debt of IDR74.57trn less cash of IDR57.31trn gives net debt of IDR17.65trn; the arithmetic gives IDR17.26trn. The model's 17.65 includes about 0.39trn of debt beyond funded debt (lease or other borrowings) that the prose does not name.
Section 3 gives OCF versus net profit for FY2024 and FY2025 only, while the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS output contract asks for a three-year accruals ratio and cash-conversion trend.

The bear case (Rp12,611) is +83% above the Rp6,875 price and no scenario prices the 4.4x de-rating the shares have held for five years; section 5 acknowledges the omission but the probability distribution stays one-sided above the market price.

flags.message: expected return +105%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return is not a discount closing. The target is a 12-month value built 60% on the P/E the shares have traded at over five years and on peers, 25% on EV/EBITDA on the same basis and only 15% on the DCF, so it assumes a partial re-rating, not convergence to intrinsic value. The arithmetic that survives the discount persisting is the earnings: at today's {{mult.FY2026E.pe|x}} FY2026E earnings the shares can rise with profit at an unchanged multiple and still pay a {{mult.FY2026E.div_yield|pct}} yield [S0, S2]. The operating facts behind the projection are the 9M2026 sales of Rp101.49trn with operating profit of Rp20.80trn, up 15% [F27, F28, S3], and net debt under one times EBITDA on cash interest of Rp4,116bn paid against Rp71,025bn of opening debt [S2 p.155]. The minority structure is valued explicitly in the bridge [S2].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'pe': 0.3, 'ev_ebitda': 0.1}
flags.justification: The DCF weight is cut to 15% because the DCF's implied exit multiple has never been the price this controlled company trades at: the own five-year average is 5.9x EV/EBITDA against 8.4x implied by the terminal value [S0, S2]. The 12-month target is anchored on the multiples the shares have actually traded at (60% P/E, 25% EV/EBITDA), and the DCF is reported as the fundamental value and explained as such in section four.
